Chào mừng bạn đến với EPS Space!

EPS là viết tắt của Earth Problem Solvers. Chúng tôi là một nhóm sinh viên đam mê không gian, khoa học và công nghệ, tận tâm giải quyết các thách thức thực tế bằng cách sử dụng dữ liệu mở và quan sát Trái Đất.

Điểm mạnh & Sở thích của chúng tôi:

- Khoa học Trái đất, Dữ liệu & Bản đồ Địa không gian (GIS)

- Phân tích dữ liệu & Giải quyết vấn đề

- Phát triển Phần mềm & Thiết kế Giải pháp

- Làm việc nhóm & Trình bày sáng tạo
summary: Nighttime Light Pollution Visualization is a satellite-based project that analyzes changes in artificial nighttime lighting using VIIRS satellite observations from 2020 to 2026, complemented by MODIS data. By applying remote sensing, GIS spatial analysis, quality filtering, and time-series trend analysis using Sen’s slope, the project identifies areas with high nighttime radiance and locations where lighting intensity is increasing or decreasing. The project aims to transform satellite observations into actionable insights that support more energy-efficient urban lighting, responsible infrastructure planning, and wildlife conservation.

PROJECT DETAILS

Project Title: NIGHTTIME LIGHT POLLUTION VISUALIZATION

Team: EPS – For a Better, Greener Planet

1. Project Overview and Objectives;

In recent years, rapid urbanization and economic development have significantly increased the use of artificial lighting at night. Streetlights, advertising signs, industrial facilities, commercial centers, and residential buildings have become essential parts of modern life. However, excessive and poorly managed lighting also creates environmental challenges. Light pollution can waste energy, affect human health, disturb wildlife behavior, and reduce the visibility of the natural night sky. These problems highlight the importance of developing effective methods to monitor and manage artificial lighting.

To address these challenges, the EPS team developed Earth at Night Explorer, an interactive Web Geographic Information System (WebGIS) designed to visualize, monitor, and analyze the global distribution of artificial nighttime lighting from 2020 to 2026. The project combines satellite remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and data analysis techniques to transform complex satellite observations into accessible maps, charts, and visual information.

The primary objective is to help users understand how artificial nighttime lighting is distributed and how it changes over time. The system allows users to compare different regions, identify areas with high nighttime brightness, analyze historical changes, and explore possible future trends.

In addition, the project aims to support environmental awareness by providing practical recommendations for smart street lighting, energy conservation, and wildlife protection.

The platform is designed for students, researchers, environmental organizations, urban planners, and the general public. Its interactive interface makes satellite information easier to understand without requiring advanced knowledge of remote sensing or GIS programming.

2. Data Sources and Methodology;

The project uses nighttime light data from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) satellite instrument, particularly its Day/Night Band (DNB). This technology can detect nighttime light emissions from Earth's surface and provides valuable information for studying the spatial distribution and changes of artificial lighting.

The dataset covers the period from 2020 to 2026, with observations organized into selected months, including March, June, September, and December, together with annual averages when data are available. Using multiple observation periods allows the system to analyze changes over time rather than relying on a single satellite image.

During data processing, satellite observations are converted into raster layers and prepared for interactive WebGIS visualization. The system uses a global raster grid of 4,008 × 2,004 pixels, corresponding to an approximate display resolution of 10 kilometers. Nighttime radiance is represented using 64 logarithmic levels to make differences between low- and high-brightness areas easier to visualize.

Radiance values are expressed in nW·cm⁻²·sr⁻¹, allowing users to compare the relative intensity of nighttime light emissions across different locations and observation periods.

In addition to nighttime light data, the project integrates satellite-derived land surface temperature information through its Thermal Surface feature. This layer allows users to examine temperature patterns across different geographical regions and compare urban areas with their surroundings.

However, land surface temperature is different from air temperature, and similarities between nighttime brightness and surface temperature do not necessarily indicate a direct cause-and-effect relationship.

The WebGIS platform was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to provide an interactive experience on both computers and mobile devices.

Artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT Plus, Claude, and Gemini, were used to support literature review, idea development, programming, code debugging, and user interface improvement. These tools assisted the development process, while the platform's geographical observations and analytical calculations are based on the project's data-processing methods.

3. Main Features and Analytical Capabilities

One of the most important features of Earth at Night Explorer is its interactive 3D globe, which allows users to rotate, zoom, and explore nighttime lighting patterns across the world.

Users can search for countries, cities, and specific locations, making it easier to examine geographical areas of interest. A timeline allows users to select observation periods between 2020 and 2026 and observe how nighttime light patterns change.

Large cities, industrial regions, and densely populated areas often display higher nighttime radiance than rural or less-developed regions. However, satellite radiance represents light detected from space rather than a direct measurement of light pollution experienced at ground level.

The Growth Analysis feature provides statistical tools for examining changes in nighttime brightness. It includes growth-index charts, year-over-year percentage changes, annual growth rates, and country rankings based on changes in nighttime radiance.

These functions help users identify regions where nighttime lighting is increasing or decreasing and highlight areas that may require further environmental investigation.

Another important feature is Trend Prediction, which presents a three-year projection of nighttime lighting based on historical observations.

The prediction method applies least-squares linear regression to the natural logarithm of annual mean radiance after adding one to the radiance value. The model uses available annual observations to estimate historical trends and extends these trends three years into the future.

The results are presented through interactive charts showing observed values, projected trends, and an 80% uncertainty interval.

This feature helps users understand possible future changes in artificial lighting and examine the uncertainty associated with trend-based projections.

Importantly; these results represent statistical scenarios rather than official forecasts. Actual future nighttime lighting may differ because of urban development, changes in lighting technology, government policies, economic conditions, and environmental factors.

The Learn & Solutions section provides educational information about the causes and consequences of light pollution, together with practical approaches to reducing unnecessary lighting.

When users select a location on the globe, the system can display nighttime radiance information, historical trends, and suggested lighting-management solutions.

The platform also includes a Cinematic Mode, which offers a visually engaging presentation of Earth's nighttime lighting and its changes over time. This feature is particularly useful for educational demonstrations, environmental communication, and project presentations.

4. Practical Applications and Proposed Solutions;

Earth at Night Explorer is designed not only to visualize satellite information but also to support discussions about sustainable lighting and environmental protection.

One important application is smart street lighting. By identifying regions with high nighttime radiance or increasing brightness, the system can help highlight areas where lighting conditions should be investigated.

Potential solutions include installing energy-efficient LED streetlights with appropriate shielding, adjusting brightness according to traffic conditions, and using motion sensors or intelligent control systems.

These approaches can reduce unnecessary electricity consumption while maintaining adequate visibility and road safety.

For commercial areas, office buildings, and advertising facilities, controlling lighting schedules is another practical solution. Reducing brightness or switching off unnecessary lights during periods of low activity can help conserve energy and limit unwanted light emissions.

The project also emphasizes wildlife conservation. Artificial light at night can disrupt the feeding, reproduction, migration, and navigation behavior of certain animal species, especially migratory birds, insects, and nocturnal wildlife.

To reduce these impacts, the team proposes limiting unnecessary lighting near forests, wetlands, coastal habitats, and other ecologically sensitive areas.

Using appropriately directed lights, reducing excessive brightness, and limiting blue-rich lighting where suitable may help protect wildlife habitats.

Through satellite-based monitoring, the platform can identify nighttime lighting patterns that may deserve further investigation. However, environmental management decisions should also consider field measurements, biodiversity information, traffic safety, and local lighting requirements.

5. Limitations; Future Development, and Project Significance

Although Earth at Night Explorer provides useful visualization and analytical tools, several limitations should be considered when interpreting its results.

VIIRS nighttime light observations can be influenced by cloud cover, snow, atmospheric conditions, sensor calibration, and changes in lighting technologies. In particular, the VIIRS Day/Night Band has limited sensitivity to some blue wavelengths emitted by modern LED lighting systems. Therefore, actual changes in artificial lighting may not always be fully reflected in satellite observations.

The platform also uses reduced-resolution raster data to improve display speed and interactive performance. As a result, some local details may be lost, making the system more suitable for regional and global comparisons than for precise assessments of individual streets or buildings.

Furthermore, the three-year prediction model is based mainly on historical radiance trends. It does not directly incorporate changes in population, economic development, urban planning, or future environmental policies.

In future development, the team aims to improve spatial resolution, expand environmental datasets, enhance statistical analysis, and provide more detailed comparisons between geographical regions.

Integrating additional information about population density, land use, biodiversity, and urban lighting policies could improve the platform's analytical capabilities and practical value.

Earth at Night Explorer demonstrates how satellite remote sensing, GIS technology, data analysis, and AI-assisted development can be combined to address a real environmental challenge.

By transforming complex satellite observations into interactive visual information, the project encourages public awareness of light pollution and supports more responsible energy use and environmental management.

With the slogan “EPS – For a Better, Greener Planet,” the team hopes to contribute to a future in which technological development, urban growth, and environmental protection can coexist sustainably.

The project's ultimate goal is to promote a simple but meaningful principle: use artificial lighting at the right place, at the right time, and at the right level.
